questions.prompt: Which statement about a p-value of 0.03 is correct?
options: The result will replicate about 97% of the time in an identical new experiment.
The effect is large because p is small, so the difference matters in practice.
There is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true given the data observed.
If there were truly no difference, data at least this extreme would occur about 3% of the time.
questions.explanation: A p-value is a probability of data given the null, not of the null given the data.

questions.prompt: 16 runs, mean 50, SD 8. Using t(15,0.975)=2.131, what is the half-width of the 95% CI for the mean? (2 decimals)
Group A mean 80, group B mean 76, both SD 8 (equal n). Cohen's d? (2 decimals)
One method has p=0.04 and another p=0.06 against the same baseline. A report says only the first 'works'. What is wrong?
options: The gap between significant and not significant is not itself significant; report effects and intervals.
p=0.06 proves that the second method does not work, so only the first one should be reported at all.
p=0.04 proves that the first method works, because it falls below the usual 0.05 threshold of significance.
Nothing is wrong: the first method crosses the threshold and the second does not, so only one works.

questions.prompt: Ten independent tests at alpha=0.05 with no real effects. Probability of at least one false positive? (3 decimals)
Welch standard error for group A (s=3, n=9) and group B (s=4, n=16): sqrt(sA^2/nA + sB^2/nB). (3 decimals)
A colleague reports 'p < 0.05, so the new controller is better.' Write what a complete report of the comparison should contain.
rubric: Effect size (difference and standardised) with a confidence interval.
Sample sizes, number of seeds, the test used and any multiple comparisons.
A statement of practical significance and a result that would reject the claim.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.
